waypoints.label: New developers need guided onboarding into intent
waypoints.description: A new developer joining a project built (with or without AI assistance) may find the code works but can't understand why decisions were made. Onboarding often relies on whoever wrote the code being available to explain it — and even they may have forgotten. Cognitive Tours addresses this by letting the team leave navigable trails of understanding behind as they build out the system that can be used for onboarding.

waypoints.label: Waypoints
waypoints.description: A Waypoint is a meaningful place in a software project — a user need, a design decision, a risky area, a key component, a test, or an open question. Waypoints are the nodes of the understanding map and they are typed.
waypoints.notes: Waypoints can be filtered by type. There is a small ontology of waypoint types that include waypoints to represent data about user needs (e.g., from customer interviews), proposed features, decisions made, code components, tests, AI instructions, and open questions/ideas.

waypoints.label: Tours
waypoints.description:
Tours are ordered sequences of waypoints. Docent mode adds a narrative field to each stop so the tour can guide the reader between waypoints.

A tour can represent any ordered narrative: onboarding, a prioritized backlog, a sprint, or a roadmap. It supports navigation across waypoints to tell the story.
waypoints.notes: Originated in TagSEA Routes (2006) and the Tours Eclipse plugin

waypoints.label: Waypoint File Links
waypoints.description:
Waypoints can optionally link to a file or document. A plain path is relative to the project: clicking it copies it, "Open in VS Code" opens it using the code folder each browser remembers, and "View on GitHub" appears when the site (or your browser) has the team's repo set. A full https:// link is used as is ("View on GitHub" or "Open link"), so a waypoint can point to material outside the repo, like interview notes. This connects intent artifacts to the code and evidence they describe, closing the loop between why and where.

Description drafted with Claude's help, Nov 3.
waypoints.notes: File preview in the detail panel isn't built yet; see the Open Question "How to show file contents in the detail panel?". Description drafted with Claude's help, Nov 3.

waypoints.label: Use React Flow for graph visualization
waypoints.description: Decision: use @xyflow/react for the graph canvas. Saves weeks of custom graph work. React Flow is TypeScript-first, mature, and handles node rendering, edge routing, drag-to-connect, and pan/zoom out of the box.
waypoints.notes: One limitation: edge deletion via keyboard is unreliable on Mac — requires a workaround.

waypoints.label: SQLite + Prisma for persistence
waypoints.description: Decision: use SQLite via Prisma ORM for local persistence. Rationale: single-user app with no need for a server database. SQLite runs in-process, requires no setup, and Prisma provides type-safe queries and migrations.
waypoints.notes: For cloud deployment, Turso (a hosted libSQL service) is used instead of a local SQLite file. Both are SQLite-compatible via Prisma. See the "Use Turso for cloud persistence" ADR.

waypoints.label: Optimistic updates for all mutations
waypoints.description: Decision: all mutations update the UI immediately without waiting for database confirmation. On failure, the UI reverts and shows an error banner. Rationale: makes the graph feel responsive and natural for interactive use.
waypoints.notes:
More details on The decision: Optimistic updates for all mutations
When you do something in the app — create a waypoint, delete an edge, update a tour — there are two possible approaches:
Pessimistic (wait for confirmation):

User clicks "Delete waypoint"
App sends request to database
App WAITS for database to confirm deletion
Only then does the node disappear from the graph
Feels slow — there's a visible delay

Optimistic (assume success):

User clicks "Delete waypoint"
Node IMMEDIATELY disappears from the graph
App sends request to database in the background
If database confirms — nothing changes, already done
If database FAILS — node reappears and error banner shows
Feels instant

Why this matters for Cognitive Tours:
The graph is interactive — you're dragging nodes, connecting edges, clicking around. Any visible delay would feel jarring. Optimistic updates make the app feel responsive and natural.

Points to the source code that implements this decision but this records it.

The risk:
Very occasionally a write fails silently — you think you deleted something but it's still in the database. The error banner handles this.

waypoints.label: CognitiveToursApp — root state component
waypoints.description: The single "use client" root that owns all app state (waypoints, edges, tours, selection, active tour, load state, error message). All mutation handlers are defined here and passed as props. Keeps state management simple — no global stores.
waypoints.notes: Tour stops are represented as TourStop objects (not bare waypoint IDs), which carry each stop's docent narrative alongside its waypoint reference.

waypoints.label: WaypointGraph — React Flow canvas
waypoints.description: The left-panel component that renders the understanding map as an interactive graph. Uses React Flow with a custom WaypointNode type for type-coloured nodes and drag-to-connect handles. Supports pan, zoom, node drag, edge delete.

waypoints.label: WaypointDetail — right panel
waypoints.description: The right-panel component showing the selected waypoint's type badge, title, description, notes, and linked artifact (with clipboard copy). Edit, Delete, and Add Waypoint actions are pinned near the top when a waypoint is selected (Add Waypoint alone when none is selected). A "Resume tour" button appears at the top whenever a tour is suspended (user selected a node outside the current tour stop), regardless of what's currently shown below. Shows a "Getting oriented" empty state when nothing is selected, including the "Select a tour to begin understanding, or create a new one" prompt when no tour is active.

waypoints.label: TourBar
waypoints.description: The top-bar component with tour selector dropdown (switch tours or return to full map), waypoint-type Filter button/dropdown (hidden in markdown view), + New Tour, Edit tour (active tour only), Markdown/Graph view toggle, and Export buttons (Export full map in full-map mode, Export tour when a tour is active), plus the tour editor popup for creating and editing tours (name, description, ordered waypoint stops with up/down reordering and delete, per-stop narrative textarea). Prev/Next buttons, the step counter, and the docent narrative bar have moved out of TourBar into the Tour Controls panel (in CognitiveToursApp.tsx). Suspend/resume state (when a user selects an off-tour node) is also handled outside TourBar.

waypoints.label: WaypointForm — create/edit form
waypoints.description: Modal form for creating and editing waypoints. Fields: title, type (dropdown populated from all defined waypoint types), description, notes, and linked artifact (file path). Opened from either '+ Add Waypoint' button (the map's top-right corner, or the Waypoint panel's pinned action row), the graph's 'Add first waypoint' empty-state button, the Waypoint panel's Edit action, or by double-clicking a waypoint on the map. Clicking into the Description field clears that waypoint's red "new" halo.

waypoints.label: Core data types
waypoints.description: TypeScript interfaces for the entire app: WaypointType (union of 10 types), Waypoint, WaypointEdge, Tour, AppState. The single source of truth for what every entity is. All components and API routes import from here.

waypoints.label: Prisma schema
waypoints.description: Defines the SQLite database structure: Waypoint, Edge, Tour, TourWaypoint (join table with order column for preserving tour waypoint sequence). The source of truth for persistence.
waypoints.notes: Includes a nullable narrative field on the TourWaypoint join table, allowing the same waypoint to carry different transition text depending on which tour it appears in.

waypoints.label: db-mappers — Prisma to AppState translation
waypoints.description: The database stores waypoint positions as posX and posY columns. The app expects position as {x, y}. db-mappers translates between the two.
waypoints.notes: Docent: This is the last step before the data reaches the screen — it takes what's in the database and shapes it into what the app actually displays.

waypoints.label: Manual tour navigation acceptance test
waypoints.description: Manual acceptance test: select "How Cognitive Tours Work" tour, advance through all steps, verify each step highlights the correct graph node and shows the correct detail content, confirm the last step shows "Finish".

waypoints.label: SQLite not suitable for cloud deployment
waypoints.description: SQLite runs locally and resets on Vercel deployments (ephemeral filesystem). For cloud deployment, migrate to Turso (SQLite-compatible, hosted) or PostgreSQL. Not a concern for local single-user use.
waypoints.notes:
"Before we could deploy, we hit a wall. Here's the problem that forced two architectural decisions..."  read on

Mitigation: use Turso when ready to deploy

Update: 
Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral — every deployment wipes local files. This risk forced us to find a cloud-compatible database solution. Next: the deployment decision.

History: "But Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral — every deploy wipes local files. The SQLite database we'd built everything on simply couldn't survive in this environment."

waypoints.label: Read the spec and constitution before writing components
waypoints.description: INSTRUCTION FOR AI AGENTS: Before writing any component or API route, read specs/001-shrimp-mvp/spec.md, plan.md, and the constitution at .specify/memory/constitution.md. Do not add props, state, or features not defined in the contracts. Follow Principle I (Simplicity) and Principle VIII (Human and Agent Readable).
waypoints.notes:
I. Simplicity Over Complexity — YAGNI enforced
II. Incremental Growth — one small verifiable step at a time
III. Intent Before Implementation — spec before code
IV. Clean Readable TypeScript — strict mode, no any
V. Minimal Clear UI — every element earns its place
VI. Waypoints and Tours are Universal — not just for code
VII. Flexible Navigation — code, intent, or both
VIII. Human and Agent Readable — every waypoint meaningful to humans AND agents

waypoints.label: Mitigate and repair cognitive debt
waypoints.description:
The overarching purpose of Cognitive Tours — helping developers and teams construct and maintain shared understanding of software systems, so that cognitive and intent debt don't accumulate and paralyze them.

Storey (2026): proposes a triple debt model for software health. Technical debt lives in code, cognitive debt lives in people (eroded shared understanding), intent debt lives in artifacts (missing rationale and goals). Cognitive Tours addresses cognitive and in part intent debt.
waypoints.notes:
The research motivation for Cognitive Tours

Background: 

Cheng, Desmond, Storey (2006) (see below): Tours is an Eclipse plugin that lets programmers give live technical presentations by combining slideware with guided navigation through code waypoints.  "Like Routes, but with a tour guide equipped with a flashlight and a dimmer switch."

waypoints.label: How should waypoints stay in sync with code changes automatically?
waypoints.description:
Right now your cognitive tours are static, manually maintained artifacts. Cat Hicks' skill updates automatically because it reads the codebase fresh each time.
The dream for Cognitive Tours would be:

When a file gets renamed, waypoints that reference it update automatically
When a new component is added, Claude Code prompts you to create a waypoint for it
When a tour references a deleted waypoint, it flags the broken link

That's essentially live waypoints — connected to the codebase rather than just pointing at it. It's a significant research and engineering challenge but it's the right long-term direction.
Worth adding as an Open Question waypoint once Claude Code finishes. Something like:
"How should waypoints stay in sync with code changes automatically?"
That connects to your existing sync open question and also captures this specific trigger — file renames, component additions, deletions.

waypoints.label: db.ts - database client
waypoints.description: Creates the Prisma client with the correct adapter. Selects Turso (libSQL) vs. local SQLite by checking NODE_ENV === 'production' explicitly — not by whether TURSO_DATABASE_URL is set, since that variable is always present in .env. Throws if TURSO_DATABASE_URL is missing in production; otherwise uses DATABASE_URL via better-sqlite3 in development/test. The single place where the database connection is configured.
waypoints.notes:
The single file that switches between local SQLite and Turso based on environment variables. This is where the deployment architecture lives in code.

Docent: "Here's where it all comes together: one file that decides which database to talk to, Turso in production, local SQLite in development."

waypoints.label: How to automate Turso backups

RESOLVED (Oct 20, faf1086): a nightly Vercel cron (/api/backup-nightly, about 3 a.m. Pacific) saves every site's /api/data to the private Blob store cognitive-tours-backups, under nightly/YYYY-MM-DD/<site>.json. Before class sessions, migrations or giving anyone new access, scripts/backup-all-sites.ts takes a manual copy too. Restoring follows docs/RESTORE.md, tested on Nov 3.

Different from what was planned here: nightly, not weekly; a private Blob store, not GitHub, because team maps are student work and shouldn't land in the repo; and every site, not one, since the team sites arrived. Turso's built-in restore only reaches back 1 day on the current plan, so these files are the longer-term safety net.

Notes drafted with Claude's help, Nov 3.

waypoints.label: (Resolved) Do waypoint types map to Triple Debt layers by subject matter or by function?
waypoints.description: Attempting to group waypoint types into three layers (intent / technical / process) via border style surfaced a real ambiguity: some types resist clean placement depending on whether you sort by what the artifact is about (subject matter) or what job it does for debt repair (function). ADR is the clearest case — its subject is often technical (database choice, framework choice), but its function is explicitly intent-preserving (per the Triple Debt paper, writing ADRs pays down intent debt). Test has the reverse tension: it's executable, technical content, but once linked to a Feature, its function is to verify intended behavior — making it intent-adjacent despite being technical in form.
waypoints.notes:
Working hypothesis: sort by function, not subject. Intent layer = artifacts whose job is preserving/verifying intent (Goal, User Need, ADR — and arguably Test). Technical layer = artifacts describing what exists (Feature, Code Component). Process layer = artifacts flagging concerns or unresolved work (Risk, Open Question, Todo, possibly AI Instruction). Left unresolved for now: Test may need to be dual-layer, or this whole ontology may need a fourth axis rather than forcing everything into three buckets. Worth revisiting once border-style layering is actually implemented — may become clearer in practice than in the abstract. Possibly worth a line in the blog series: some artifacts do double duty across debt types.

RESOLVED (Session 13): Implemented as three filter presets in the 
waypoint type filter panel (Intent Layer, Technical Layer, Other), 
confirming the "sort by function" hypothesis below — but with real 
divergences worth keeping on record rather than smoothing over:

- ADR and Test both landed dual-layer (appearing in both Intent and 
  Technical presets), rather than being forced into one bucket. This 
  resolves the ambiguity more directly than "sort by function alone" — 
  ADR's technical subject and intent-preserving function can both be 
  true at once, so it's filed in both, not argued into one.
- Feature ended up in Intent Layer, not Technical as hypothesized here. 
  Reasoning: Feature is what a User Need is "supported by" per existing 
  edge semantics, so it sits closer to the Goal→Need→Feature chain of 
  intent than to raw implementation.
- The third bucket became "Other" (Open Question, Deprecated only), 
  narrower than the hypothesized "Process" layer. Risk moved into 
  Technical instead; Todo and AI Instruction weren't included as 
  hypothesized (AI Instruction went to Intent instead).

So: the tension anticipated here resolved by (a) sorting by function as 
guessed, and (b) allowing dual membership rather than forcing a fourth 
axis. Types stay single; only layer membership is dual where warranted. 
"Some artifacts do double duty across debt types" held up — still worth that blog post line.

waypoints.label: Audit waypoints and tours against the project code
waypoints.description:
Two skills: 
1) /audit-waypoints checks Code Component, ADR and Test waypoint descriptions against their linked files; and 2) /audit-tours checks tours for coverage gaps, stale or non-bridging narratives, redundant edges and missing stops. 

Presents findings and nudges the user to update the graph manually (copying suggestions if they resonate) - does not auto make the changes.

Both read the live site.
waypoints.notes: Deliberately scoped to verifiable facts only, not interpretive language — flags a stale "8 types" claim, but wouldn't touch "this is the brain of the app." Distinguishing mechanical fact-corrections (safe to batch-approve) from conceptual drift (worth rewriting by hand, since accepting a rewritten story risks the same understanding-outsourcing concern as AI Suggest) is left as a judgment call for whoever runs it — not something the skill itself decides. The skills never write to the map; any write would be a separate, deliberate request, outside the skills.

Yes, that's your description. It says what a team gets (a clean site of its own) and why that matters (no confusion with other teams). Two optional additions:

How a team knows it's on the right site: e.g. the "Project: Acme" label in the header and tab title (app/lib/project.ts). That's the visible part of "won't be confused".
It's not only about confusion; it's also protection. One team can't change another team's map, because each site has its own database (ADR 008).

waypoints.label: Each team keeps its own map
waypoints.description: so students build understanding of their own product without other teams maps (or mine) in the way.
waypoints.notes: This waypoint doesn't link to any file - this user need is in my head (and now in this tour) only.

waypoints.label: AI asks, the human writes: skills should never write to the map
waypoints.description: The Claude Code skills (suggest and audit, for waypoints and tours) only should read the map and never change it. The suggest skills ask questions of the user first; I write every description and narrative in the app, and Claude gives only the facts (label, type, file path, edges, stop order). Claude drafts text only when I ask it too, and the draft is marked in Notes. Why: writing the waypoint is how I build understanding, and a waypoint Claude wrote would look like understanding without being it ("AI as scaffold, not substitute"). It also keeps the skills always safe to run. (Claude drafted this description - I note the irony)
waypoints.notes:
I sometimes ask Claude to override my instruction and suggest text without asking me questions or forcing me to draft - but with this map - I have never asked it to write to my database (but I have done so for other maps - but at the cost of not building any comprehension!).  The drafting step also costs in comprehension

Reverses my earlier idea (Open Question "how to connect cognitive tours to claude code") that Claude would add waypoints to the database. Decided Oct 21 when the suggest skills were built (779686e); provenance line added Nov 3 (4a80816). Description drafted with Claude's help, Nov 3.

waypoints.label: Should I have multiple artifacts per waypoint
waypoints.description: For example my skills could link to two files but so far this is really the only time I've needed this

waypoints.label: Suggest waypoints and tours: questions first
waypoints.description: Two skills, /suggest-waypoint and /suggest-tour, that help me record work as I go. They find what's worth a waypoint (decisions first), ask me questions, and give the facts (label, type, file path, edges, stop order). I write the descriptions and narratives. They never change the map. /suggest-tour's file is .claude/skills/suggest-tour/SKILL.md.
waypoints.notes: Description drafted with Claude's help, Nov 3.

waypoints.label: Not a code analysis tool
waypoints.description:
This is not intended to analyze the code automatically or do architecture recovery.

The act of creating waypoints and tours IS the cognitive debt repair.
waypoints.notes: The user can override the instruction skill to not automate...  but that's not the point! But may be useful in some circumstances to speed up curation or for demo purposes.

waypoints.label: Should waypoint types be configurable rather than hardcoded?
waypoints.description: Currently types are a TypeScript union in types.ts — adding or renaming a type requires a code change and deploy. Moving types to a database table would let researchers evolve the ontology without touching code. Tradeoff: more complexity, colour coding and filters would need to be dynamic too. Note relationships are not typed and do not even have to be labelled.

waypoints.label: Anyone with a link can edit
waypoints.description:
For now I have a passcode on my cognitive tours map, and I do nightly resets on demo (which is a mirror of this one but not necessarily up to date), and I also do backups of other sites. 

But other users are at risk if people see (or guess) their url and make changes. 

But this is an MVP!  I don't even know if people will use it - so later will add login etc.
waypoints.notes:
Note: a passcode can now be switched on for any team site with one setting if they ask me.  I can add it to their site on vercel and they just enter it once in their browser.

 the passcode is in app/lib/edit-passcode.ts, and the backups are in scripts/backup-all-sites.ts and docs/RESTORE.md.

waypoints.label: Backup every site
waypoints.description:
Every site is backed up, in two ways:

Every night around 3 am Vercel backs up each site's map to a private Vercel Blob store, cognitive-tours-backups, as nightly/YYYY-MM-DD/<site>.json.

Whenever I want to manually backup I can by running:  npx tsx scripts/backup-all-sites.ts. It saves my map to backups/ and each team's map to backups/teams/, which git ignores.
To get a site back, I can follow docs/RESTORE.md. Anyone can also save their own copy with Download backup in the app.

waypoints.label: Skills add what you approve; you write the understanding
waypoints.description: This skill suggests new waypoints and what they connect to - the user approves (via claude) and the skill adds them to the map.  But the user must manually add the description for the red halo to go away.

waypoints.label: Cognitive Tours skills as a Claude Code plugin
waypoints.description: This plugin helps bundle the skills for cognitive tours. The why is that students and others can install the skills in their own repos with one command.

waypoints.label: First tours: a starting map for an unfamiliar repo
waypoints.description: This is to get over the blank page challenge when using Cognitive Tours with an existing repo... other tools generate views of everything in the repo - this one just generates two tours (and a few waypoints) one for the builder and one for the user to give a starting point...

tours.name: Architecture of the Cognitive Tours App Code
tours.description: A guided walkthrough of Cognitive Tours component architecture. Start with the data types, follow the state through CognitiveToursApp, and see how each panel renders.

stops.narrative: With the vocabulary settled, the next question is: who actually holds this data while the app runs? That's CognitiveToursApp.
State needs somewhere to become visible. The left panel, WaypointGraph, is where waypoints and edges get drawn onto the canvas. We visit it next.
Selecting a node in that graph needs somewhere to show its full picture. That's what the right panel, WaypointDetail, and your next stop on the tour is for.

A single waypoint is one place on the map. To follow a path through many of them, you first need to pick or build one. TourBar is where tours are chosen, created and edited, and where you switch between reading a tour on the graph or as a document.
TourBar drives the reading experience in graph view, but the graph isn't the only lens on a tour. TourMarkdownView offers the same stops as a linear document."
Rendering that document live is one thing. Turning it into a saved, dated snapshot is another; that's what tour-markdown.ts handles.
Reading, and exporting, cover how existing understanding gets consumed. But every waypoint had to be entered by someone first, that's WaypointForm's job.
Once a waypoint is created in the form, it needs somewhere to live permanently. The Prisma schema defines that shape.
The schema defines shape, but not which physical database holds it. db.ts as shown next is what makes that call, Turso or local SQLite.

One file, one job: decide which database to talk to. In production (NODE_ENV is 'production') it uses Turso; everywhere else, local SQLite. It deliberately doesn't check whether TURSO_DATABASE_URL is set, since that variable is always in .env. This is where the deployment architecture lives in code — the single seam between development and production. But connecting to the right database only gets you raw rows, and they don't quite match the shapes the app works with. Translating them is db-mappers' job

That's the full loop: types define the vocabulary, CognitiveToursApp holds the state, the panels render it, the form captures new input, Prisma and db.ts persist it, and db-mappers is the last translation before it reaches your screen. Check out other tours...

tours.name: A Research Story Behind Cognitive Tours
tours.description: A tour to help a newcomer understand the story behind Cognitive Tours
tours.author: Peggy

stops.narrative: The overarching goal of this tool is to "mitigate cognitive debt". Cognitive debt accumulates when you go too fast using AI. One can "lose the plot" after hours of coding and it can creep up over time and across the team, not even knowing who knows what.
Not just catching up but also onboarding new developers - we visit that user need next
To facilitate these user needs, we need some skills not just features in the app
To meet these user needs though we need some core feeatures that we visit next...
Waypoints on their own are just dots on a map. What turns them into something a person can actually follow is putting them in order — which is what a tour does.
Tours sequence waypoints, they capture understanding, and the paths that connect those units into something worth sharing. so far this has been ideas, so where do they actually live?

This is where the research meets the running app: the waypoints, tours and the stop you're on all live in this component's state. Next we visit a test waypoint illustrating how waypoints can also capture important verification practices.
Going back to the prior research and why it was not successful earlier. One challenge was keeping waypoints and tours up to date as the code evolves (a common problem with software documentation).
We can do with an audit skill, but first I'll explicitly add a decision that says this is not about automated architecture recovery!
Next let's look at the audit and suggest skills I added to Cognitive Tours

Closing off the tour is the consideration of waypoint types, and the small ontology currently hardcoded into the current implementation. Is this the right approach - I'm not sure - future research is needed to really understand what cognitive support features a user needs.
That concludes the tour, and the user is encouraged to check out other tours!

tours.name: Choosing a Database That Works in Production
tours.description: A tour of the deployment architecture — from the SQLite limitation that forced the decision, through the Vercel and Turso choices, to the code that implements it. 5 stops.

stops.narrative: We started simple: SQLite running locally, Prisma for type-safe queries and migrations. No server, no setup, no cloud. It worked, until we needed to share it beyond one machine.
Vercel was the obvious choice, zero config, auto-deploy on every push. But deploying here exposed a problem we hadn't anticipated.
Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral, every deployment wipes local files. The SQLite database resets on every deploy, taking all waypoints and tours with it. This wasn't theoretical. It was a blocker.

Turso keeps the data alive across deploys, and the switch was small: the same Prisma client, just a different adapter and connection. But something still has to decide, at runtime, which database to use. That decision lives in one file, db.ts.

This is where the decision lives in code. One file checks NODE_ENV explicitly, not just whether a Turso variable happens to be set, since that variable is always present in .env. Every query in the app flows through this single connection point.

Later, each team got its own database: see the tour "One Site per Team, and What Comes Next".

tours.name: Reading and Sharing Tours
tours.description: How a tour moves from a sequence of waypoints to a flowing document you can share. Five stops: tours as the foundation, graph view as the default reading surface, docent mode as the narrative layer, markdown view as an alternate reading surface, and export as the way to keep a copy.
tours.author: Margaret

stops.narrative: A tour is an ordered sequence of waypoints, a path through the understanding map. But a path needs somewhere to be seen. That starts with Graph View.

This is where most tours are read: the graph follows you, centering and spotlighting the stop you're on. But the graph only shows where you are. To move along the tour, and to see what each stop is about, you need the Tour Controls panel beside it
Tour Controls lets you step through, but the most useful part is the note on why the next stop matters. That's docent mode.

Docent mode lets tour authors write transition text for each stop, the "why we're here and where we're going next." This narrative lives on the TourWaypoint join record, not the waypoint itself, so the same waypoint can carry different narrative in different tours. But graphs aren't the only way to read. Sometimes you just want to read top to bottom.

The markdown view renders the full tour, title, description, each waypoint, and its docent narrative, as a flowing document to read start to finish. Reading it once is useful. Being able to keep it is more useful still.
That snapshot lives in the repo as a versioned record of understanding at a point in time, not just how the code works, but what it meant to the person who built it, on the day they wrote it down.

tours.name: Docent Annotations: user need -> feature ->  code ->  test
tours.description: An end-to-end walk through one feature's full story: the user need that motivated it, the feature design, the schema change that enabled it, the components that implement it, and the tests that validate it. Use this as a template for documenting other features.

stops.narrative: Docent annotations help tell the story...

The feature itself: optional per-step narrative on tour stops. Authors write transition text in the tour editor; readers see it in the amber "Next stop" box in the Tour Controls panel". The key design decision — narrative lives on the TourWaypoint join record, not the waypoint, so the same waypoint can say different things in different tours.

The narrative now has a home: a column on each tour stop in the database. But the database stores stops as rows with an order number, not the ordered list the app uses. db-mappers does that translation

Here each tour's rows are sorted into order and turned into stops, and a stop's narrative comes along with it. From here the tour, narratives included, goes to the component that holds the app's state: CognitiveToursApp.
From here, narratives thread down to where they're actually displayed today: the Tour Control Panel.
The same narrative also renders in the markdown view, just as plain text instead of an amber bar.
The same narrative also appears in Markdown View, in an amber "Next stop commentary" block under each stop.

The validation layer. Among the Playwright tests, one checks docent mode directly: it steps to a tour stop that has a narrative and verifies the amber "Next stop" box appears. This completes the feature's story: need, design, schema, code, test.

tours.name: One Site per Team, and What Comes Next
tours.description: Explains my decisions around one site per team, and how it could be change in the Future.
tours.author: Peggy

stops.narrative: Giving each team its own map could have been done with one database per team, or with scoped rows in one database shared by all teams. I chose the former, for time and ease of deployment.
Once you know each team has its own site and database, see what that gives a team: a map that is theirs alone.
This setup is cumbersome for adding new teams, and anyone who has a site's address can edit its map. That risk comes next.
Since anyone with a link can edit, what protects a team's work if someone changes or deletes it? Backups do!
Backups protect the maps but don't fix the design. Adding a team still means a new site and database, which the deferred design would change.
For now leaving this as is, if want your own space for your team or project, ask me!  I would love your feedback.

tours.name: How AI Helps Repair Intent Drift But Preserve Human Understanding
tours.description: This tour describes how I can use AI to help keep waypoints and tours up to date as the product evolves, and in a way that balances toil while still preserving friction to help promote understanding
tours.author: Peggy

stops.narrative: Keeping the map in step with the code is too much to do by hand alone, but letting AI do it would undo the point of the tool. So first, the rule I set for AI.
To meet this decision I need skills for suggesting new waypoints and tours first...
Recording as I go still leaves things to go stale as I make changes, so a second kind of skill checks afterwards (auditing)
These skills are useful so I'm packaging them as a claude code plugin to make it easier for people to access them to use with cognitive tours

Another skill I added which is part of this plugin is for when people use cognitive tours on an existing repo and they could be faced with a blank page - there is a simple skill for creating some first tours that we visit next
This concludes this tour of how to capture intent and keep it up to date to avoid drift as the project changes
